Torchlight, developed by Runic Games and released in 2009, is a hack'n'slash steeped in the tradition of genre classics, and for good reason, as it was crafted by former Blizzard North developers, the minds behind the legendary Diablo series. With its smooth gameplay, vibrant steampunk-fantasy aesthetic, and incredibly rich content, this is a gripping and memorable title, perfect for diving into the genre.

You play as an adventurer in the mining village of Torchlight, tasked with thwarting the corruption of Ember, a magical resource, and uncovering the secrets of Ordrak, a malevolent dragon-like entity. Quests (slaying key monsters, collecting specific items, etc.) and dialogues with NPCs like Syl, Vasman, Trill-Bot, or Hatch push you deeper into sprawling dungeons. Syl guides the main storyline, while Vasman, Trill-Bot, and Hatch add lore through side quests. Simple yet immersive and charming, the story fuels the adventure, though action takes center stage.

You choose from three distinct character classes, each with unique looks and abilities. The Destroyer, a brute excelling in melee combat, is perfect for fans of raw power. The Vanquisher, an agile sharpshooter, wields bows, pistols, rifles, or traps. The Alchemist, a mage, casts attack spells or summons creatures.

Your adventure begins in the village of Torchlight, a colorful and welcoming hub filled with quaint buildings and friendly inhabitants. The NPCs are diverse: merchants sell weapons, potions, or special items; an enchanter boosts your gear (with a risk of breaking it); and the aforementioned quest-givers provide missions. But the true secrets lie in Torchlight’s depths, ready to quench your thirst for adventure.

Torchlight’s underbelly teems with procedurally generated dungeons, each with a captivating atmosphere. The Orden Mines, located just beneath Torchlight, form a network of damp, grimy tunnels sparkling with Ember crystals, scattered with abandoned carts and skeletons, remnants of a bygone mining era. The Necropolis and crypts plunge you into a macabre atmosphere, filled with tombs, sarcophages, and eerie ancient murals. The Estherian Ruins reveal crumbling ancient cities, where wild nature intertwines with broken statues, evoking a lost glory. The Tu’Tara Caverns dazzle with their humid galleries, adorned with luminescent mushrooms, colorful plants, and suspended bridges, home to warrior tribes. The Molten Prison exudes suffocating heat, with incandescent walls and bubbling lava all around; it’s simply hellish. The Lost Fortress impresses with its collapsed ramparts and once-majestic halls, now overrun by creatures. The Black Palace, with its gothic air, intrigues with sinisterly ornate corridors and a mysterious aura. The Corrupted Realms, marked by cracked floors and pulsing Ember veins, glow with reddish hues, reflecting Ordrak’s corruption. Finally, the Lair, Ordrak’s ultimate stronghold, imposes a dark, chaotic ambiance. Every setting is rich in detail, a feast for the eyes, making each exploration unforgettable.

Torchlight’s gameplay is intuitive, as any great hack'n'slash should be. Slaughter hordes of enemies, loot gold, weapons, potions, identification scrolls, and town portal scrolls, and enhance your skills through a simple three-tab skill tree (offensive, defensive, utility). XP and Fame unlock points to boost strength, dexterity, defense, or magic. Combat is frenetic, the loot is addictive, but the limited inventory can be a hassle, thankfully, your pet handles selling excess items. Procedurally generated dungeons offer near-infinite replayability, though quests (kill, fetch) can feel repetitive. The endgame is robust thanks to side quests, and moddability, with new levels, items, and content created by the community, is a real strength.

As for weapons, there’s something for everyone. Swords, axes, hammers, wands, bows, pistols, rifles, crossbows… The selection is massive, with two interchangeable weapon sets. You could pair a bow with a rifle, a heavy sword with a crossbow, or dual pistols with light melee weapons; the possibilities are vast. Embedding gems in weapons adds stat bonuses. Ranged weapons make fights easier and are super fun, but melee’s raw power is thrilling too.

The pet (dog or cat) is a brilliant addition: it fights by your side, carries loot, and sells items in the village. Equip it with spells (ideally attack or healing) and amulets. Charming and useful, it’s a real asset.

A fishing mini-game in dungeons (click at the right moment) lets you catch fish that grant buffs (speed, mana, etc.) or temporarily transform your pet into a game creature, like a Varkolyn, Elemental, or Mimic, with unique abilities for 120 to 3600 seconds, depending on the fish’s size. Sometimes, you loot random gear, like boots. Fun but somewhat minor, fishing adds a unique touch to a highly codified genre.

The bestiary is a festival of diverse creatures: rats, spiders, trolls, blobs, skeletons, zombies, specters, goblins, dragons, and more. Bosses, like Krag, punctuate most chapters and demand tactical play.

The soundtrack, composed by Matt Uelmen (of Diablo 1 and 2 fame), is pure delight, with acoustic melodies blending guitars, flutes, and percussion, majestically accompanying each biome. Torchlight’s theme, soft and nostalgic, is an instant classic. Sound effects and voice acting, though subtle, are polished.

Torchlight is a rich and charming hack'n'slash. Its intuitive gameplay, colorful settings, enchanting music, fun bestiary, and handy pets make it a standout classic. Perfect for newcomers and solid for Diablo-like fans, I wholeheartedly recommend Runic Games’ gem to everyone!

Torchlight. A game developed and published by Runic Games.

I am deeply invested in the ARPG genre, and constantly strive for a new game that would satiate my ever growing hunger in this field. Torchlight was one of those games. It had everything i was looking for, from game play style, to the visuals and even the atmospheric level design. Coming from titles such as Grim Dawn and Diablo 3 was definitely a learning curve and we will cover why down below.

[h1]Story 5/10[/h1]
Torchlight in no aspect reinvents the wheel, it only builds upon an already familiar and well loved mechanic, you run in, you kill things, you loot their gear and use that gear to kill bigger things and rinse and repeat until you are a God. It's story is no different, A relatively cliche story line that very barely covers a reason to delve into these caves and fight hordes of unrelenting horrors, but never the less you do and the story does begin to unfold the further down you go, but never really offers you anything groundbreaking at all. It's well written and the dialogue is entertaining but the depth and intrigue i look for in most RPG's as a whole now is almost completely lacking here.

[h1]Gameplay 5/10[/h1]
[b]+ Environments:[/b] One thing that has to be said about Torchlight is its development of environments. The world has been painstakingly designed to offer you a certain atmosphere with every step. You'll never feel as though the area is irrelevant or boring because of how unique each map is and can be as a whole.
[b]+ Characters:[/b] Much akin to the original Diablo there are only 3 classes here, Destroyer, Vanquisher and Alchemist (Essentially Warrior, Archer and Mage, for those of you keeping score). Now i know "Only 3 classes, that sounds like a negative?!" And it would be truthfully, but here it works and its works as well as you could hope for. Each of the 3 classes comes with their own set of trees to level up (3 Each) which really helps diversify the characters and gives a "unique" element to everyone's individual character.
[b]+/- Stats/Scaling:[/b] Torchlight neither nails it nor fails it the stat system, Although the levelling system in terms of stats works well from a purely mathematical standpoint, it doesn't really offer much in practice. 50 points into Strength will make you hit a lot harder, but the enemies on each floor are levelling with you, so the change is almost unnoticeable. Which is why i had to give it a mixed rating because although its done and allows you to "level" something, its almost completely useless as Armour and Weapons will be what define your damage, not your stats.
[b]- Movement:[/b] And here is where things get a little messy. The movement in this game despite being almost entirely mouse controlled is extremely clunky and often gets confusing to use. There are very limited amounts of movement skills that allow you traverse the maps easier but they vary vastly in usefulness.
[b]- Enemy Variations:[/b] In short, there aren't a lot and most just feel like a re-skinned version of the last. Very few enemies offer any sort of interesting ability or random effect that would spark some kind of "Oh that was different" remarks. But no, there really isn't a lot here and what is here is rather bland.
[b]- Loot Drops and Inventory:[/b] I chose to put both loot and inventory into the same negative column because they go hand in hand. The inventory space in this game is a joke, Most of the armour or weapons you find require identify scrolls to even become useful which also take up your already limited inventory, And then on top of that completely useless and under levelled gear will continue to drop for you well into 20 levels lower than you. Couple that with the fact that most of the armour you will find will be for the other 2 classes and not your own. It's definitely a frustrating experience..

[h1]Visuals 7/10[/h1]
In spite of its age, Torchlight actually has stayed relatively fresh and visually pleasing, It's far from a graphical phenom by any exaggeration but due to its cartoon style graphical quality and design it has aged extremely well. There was no significant drops in frames in the entire time i played, nor was there any minor or major graphical issues during this time either. The game has been designed extremely well and looks the part.

[h1]Audio 7/10[/h1]
Much akin to the visual segment of this review, the Audio has as well aged extremely well, Offering a crisp and delightful soundtrack perfectly scored for the game, and a set of minor although pleasing sound effects that will sound out as you complete your adventure here. Again there were no minor or major audio issues, and it remained crisp and clean the entire playthrough.

[h1]Overall 6/10 "Imperfect" [/h1]
Whilst not groundbreaking in any aspect at all, Torchlight is at its core fundamental, a very decent and well made game. Some of its mechanics are extremely outdated and are reminiscent almost entirely of Diablo 1. The world is interesting but almost devoid of any kind of history and lore, The characters and classes are well thought out and work well in the schematic of the game, but are limited by the clunky style of motion that it provides. Torchlight is a game i'd pick up on sale and not at full price, Because as interesting as it is, its missing a lot that i would expect by today's standards.

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
Torchlight is a Top-Down Action RPG Dungeon Crawler developed by Runic Games in 2009. The game invokes a Diablo-esque / Fate-esque gameplay mechanic mostly because the developers were former members of the teams that made said Diablo and Fate games.

[h1]PLOT (No Spoilers):[/h1]
The game is set on the town of Torchlight, a small mining community who stumbled across a strange new mineral called 'Ember' which produces an unfortunate side effect to anyone who comes into contact with a corrupt piece. The player takes on the roles of the Alchemist, the Vanquisher or the Destroyer who makes their way through the deep mines and caves of Torchlight to stop a great evil from rising and destroying the world.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Classical Formula: -(Also a CON, see below) Although the game is dangerously familiar to Diablo, Torchlight executes this formula almost to perfection. The loot system, monsters, player classes and gameplay mechanic were applied and utilized very well in a way that gives a renewed interest on the genre.

+ Artistic: -Graphically, its not the most pleasing game, but its true artistic quality is with the style. It deviates from the regular dark, gothic themes of most games in the genre and instead, replaces it with a cartoon look in a steam punk setting.

+ Map Variety: -Story wise, you're only headed down, but each map you enter has completely different themes. You can be exploring a dark dank cave one moment, and the next, find yourself in a long forgotten stone crypt or an ancient temple.

+ Sound and Music: -The composer is Matt Uelman, Composer for works such as Diablo, World of Warcraft and Star Craft, and with a track like that, you can only expect greatness in the music quality.

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- No Multiplayer: - The game is a single player experience. No multiplayer mode whatsoever which disappointed many fans.

- Story: - Rather weak and forgettable story with too few side missions.

- Classical Formula: -(Also a PRO, see above), Strip it down to its bare minimum and you have a generic Diablo Clone right down to the Story. PERSONALLY, I think its GOOD since the newer generation of gamers who never got to experience the glory of the original Diablo can now experience it through Torchlight.

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
[b]GREAT GAME FOR GREAT VALUE.[/b] Although some may argue that Torchlight (1) is obsolete because of the release of Torchlight II, the first title still provides a lot of entertaining hours with its Diablo (1) type of gamestyle.

[h1]WORTH IT?:[/h1]
Sale or full price, this game deserves your attention however, you may also want to check out [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/41500/]Torchlight 2[/url] since it expands the world and introduces multiple new classes.

[h1]FINAL NOTES:[/h1]
You would think that its just your average Dungeon Crawler RPG and you would be right since all the elements of Torchlight are the basic elements to an Action RPG, HOWEVER, it's how Torchlight merges those elements that make it stand out from the rest. From start to finish, this game uses and applies the tried and tested classical formula to create a wonderful and memorable experience.

I don't really play games like [i]Torchlight[/i]. The style of action RPG proliferated by titles like [i]Diablo[/i] never really interested me. It's mostly just a repetitive slog of killing and looting identical enemies who changed only statistically, becoming incrementally more difficult so as to retain the same amount of effort required for their deaths. While [i]Torchlight[/i] is all that and more, it managed to keep me entertained for quite some time through diverse enemy types, artistic direction and engaging skill trees.

The gameplay hardly needs explaining - it's like [i]Diablo[/i]. You control most everything in the game using the mouse and some hotkeys. I chose to play as the 'vanquisher' class, focusing on ranged weaponry and magic related to it. The abilities of this class mostly serve to complement her ranged weapons, and I managed to completely finish the game without even equipping a melee weapon. I did find that the class benefited significantly from having summoning spells, allowing players to fire powerful ranged spells at enemies while minions keep them at bay. A lot of the more powerful weapons felt great to use, and I was impressed by the game's lenience toward players interested in multiple gameplay styles--nothing stopped me from summoning an army of skeletons, even though I didn't choose the class focused on that at the start of the game.

[i]Torchlight[/i]'s balancing feels fine, though later levels do feature some enemies with huge damage output that were a pain to get past. I really liked the way the game's entire story takes place in a single dungeon, with the player's gradual descent into the earth beneath the titular town slowly revealing different fortresses and ancient ruins all lying beneath the ground. The game begins with entry into the mine upon which Torchlight's economy is reliant upon, but before the game's end you'll see a sprawling necropolis, colourful, flooded ruins and a fiery dwarven fortress. The graphical diversity keeps things interesting, and everything's quite pretty too. I liked the cartoony art style, but I found it quite curious how many enemies were simply recoloured, buffed up a bit and reused.

On release, some criticised [i]Torchlight[/i] for it's lack of any form of multiplayer component. I personally found this to be a good decision, as a single-player game tends to be more focused. [i]Torchlight[/i], despite the admirable streamlining of UI and gameplay still contains a large amount of engaging content, even after the final boss. I just don't know if [i]Torchlight[/i] will be one of those games that the average player can get a huge amount of mileage out of--while I found the content to be sufficient, it certainly does get old after a certain point.

At its heart beats a quick-based action RPG where performing story based kill or fetch quests, see you fighting through numerous levels of varying monsters and enemy bosses. Torchlight is an action RPG, made by some of the guys who did Diablo 1 and 2. That is practically where the similarities end, however, as this world is much brighter than the Diablo games, and does not have quite the same level of complexity in terms of builds, etc.

The story is pretty generic - town is being overrun and you must dive into the caves and save the world, etc. You certainly won't be playing this game for plot. There are three classes available - Destroyer, Vanquisher and Alchemist (again, quite standard for an action RPG). The skill tree and points do allow for a fair amount of variety, and itemisation also plays a big role, with set items being particularly useful.

I also found the endless dungeon system to be particularly engaging, as the floors go on forever and get progressively more difficult the further you go. This is where you will spend your time - the end game - once you have finished the story mode. The heirloom system was also a very nice touch: you can "retire" a character, and choose one of their items to pass on to a new character, upgrading it significantly in the process. The ability to mod the game, changing almost every aspect of it, is also a big positive and really adds to the experience - highly recommended to get some mods and try them out.

One thing to bear in mind before purchasing: there is no multiplayer functionality whatsoever - you will be playing this solo, and it did get a little tedious for me after a while.

Recommended for those looking for something casual, and for those who enjoy their action RPGs.

Made from Ex Blizzard staff, torchlight is a hack and slash that has you delve into the dungeons below the town to destroy creatures corrupted by ember and stop an evil force from destroying the world. You can pick from 3 different classes that match what was available in Diablo (a Warrior, Rouge and Magic user, though they are renamed to the Destroyer, Vanquisher and Alchemist).

While offering many of the same options as diablo, it does have a few differences that sets it apart. While each dungeon is random (same as Diablo) and the characters skill progressions works much the same as Diablo 2 (some skills feed other skills) you do have a few new options. Your character can have a pet assigned, that helps by sending loot back to down. There is a fishing minigame where the characters can use the fish they capture for different effects, and to transform their pet into something different. You can at any point retire your hero, which grants an heirloom to your new character with some of their skills and stats, which in effect servers as a new game+ mode (which can be accessed at any time as once you pick a difficulty level its locked for that character.

The difficulty varies wildly, depending on which class and skills you pick up, what loot you find, and the base difficulty. I played the Destroyer and found it quite fun and his skills were quite useful and suited for my play style, however on the hardest difficulty kiting was needed to progress. It got to a point where I was only able to kill a few monsters, retreat/heal before jumping back into the fray, as before my character was wading through an entire level of monsters and rarely using healing items. I’m not sure if I was under leveled for the area or needed better loot, but it got hard fast in a way that diablo never did. Don’t even get me started on the end boss. That was a nightmare.

The game offers native support for custom mods, which can be accessed at any point from the town map.

Graphically the game looks like a cuter version of Diablo- everything looks cartoony. The game isn’t aiming for a dark and depressing feel so the tone works quite well (even if you are trekking through Ruins, Crypts and other gloomy places). Similarly, the music and sound is the same, instead of screams and roars of creatures you get grunts and the effects of weapons clashing over the top of a relatively mild music score (again think of the Diablo music score with a lot of string instruments). A lot of the enemies are just reskins, with more hit points and extra abilities as you go deeper. I think the total amount of unique enemies (not including the re-skinned variants) sits somewhere between diablo 1 and 2 (but closer to 1).

You can gamble loot, and enchant items much like the Diablo series, and there are hatch quests to do if you want to take a break from the standard dungeon. If you have an itch to play something Diablo-ish but don’t want to play diablo then this is the game for you

If you are chasing 100% achievements then expect to become a master of this with multiple runs required, 5 hours speed runs, very hard hardcore mode, a run from each character type, hatch quest plus requiring mods to be installed.

Yes, I'm aware that Torchlight is a "Very Positive" game, but that does not make it immune to criticism. I didn't write this review simply to be a contrarian jerk. 

Videogames age, some more than others. At times, all it takes is for a game to receive a sequel, in order for its age to become readily apparent. Torchlight II improves on the original in every conceivable way. I'll even go as far as to say that Torchlight has been rendered obsolete. There's literally no reason to play Torchlight 1 over its sequel, or over the great many other loot-heavy action RPGs that have been released over the years.

The absolute biggest problem with this game is the difficulty curve. I played through this game on normal, and for 9/10ths of the game, there wasn't any challenge. However, once I got to the final portion of the game, I started running into Dark Zealots. Dark Zealots have auto-targeting instant lightning. All it takes is a couple crits and I die. I admit that my lightning resistance wasn't up to snuff, but the fact that this attack is completely unavoidable is ridiculous. Once Dark Zealots start appearing, they're bound to show up fairly often throughout the post-game. I was on the 5th floor of the Shadow Vault and a Dark Zealot's lightning brought me from full health to death. 

I played through Torchlight II on hard difficulty. A veteran is likely to pop in here and say "That's still way too easy." but hear me out. Torchlight II on hard was more consistent than Torchlight 1 on normal. The game remained fairly challenging (for me) throughout the entirety of the main campaign. I didn't sleepwalk through the game, nor did I suddenly get a heaping helping of horse manure towards the end of it and beyond.

By the way, why does Ordrak have 3 billion HP? Why can he summon countless dragons and skeletons? I'm positively boggled that anyone signed off on this nonsense of a finale. The ludicrousness of the final boss really stands out, when every other boss dies in a minute or two. Torchlight 2 was more consistent when it came to bosses.

Loot. Now I know it's difficult to expect good loot. There is the almighty RNG, and I've never been very lucky. Nevertheless, there is a rhyme and reason to how this system should work, and players should feel like their time is rewarded, especially when they defeat bosses or discover secret rooms. Instead, you're just as likely to get a weapon that's usable for half the game as you are to not find any decent armor upgrades for 3/4s of the game. AGAIN, Torchlight II is more consistent. 

Torchlight II also has better quest-design, exploration, map-design, classes, skills, monster-variety, and so on and so forth. It's practically a revelation by comparison. 

Now I could download a couple mods to fix the Dark Zealot's insane lightning, or drop Ordrak's HP to something manageable, or improve the myriad of other things that need improving, but that's not my idea of a fun time. Mods are at their best when they add to a game, not just fix its problems. Besides, I already own the sequel. At this point, there really isn't an excuse not to. Torchlight II enjoys sizable discounts during all of the major Steam sales.

On the bright side, when I review Torchlight II (eventually); I won't have to spend the entirety of it discussing why it's a better game than the prequel.

It seems that when a new genre springs into being, that’s when the biggest deluge of imitators tends to appear. That was certainly the case if you look at the field of ARPGs, as a huge number of them rose in the shadow of the original Diablo rather than either of its sequels. Torchlight wasn’t a contemporary of Diablo but even coming a decade later the influence is clear, and unsurprising given the talent behind it at Runic Games. It followed the pattern so faithfully, in fact, that it failed to innovate in ways that have allowed other ARPGs to flourish in the same period. That’s not to say Torchlight is a bad game, but rather one where the gulf between it and better games is evident.

The town of Torchlight was founded atop an enormous vein of ember, a pretty standard mystical mineral that can enchant or corrupt things depending on what the plot requires. Mining the stuff was going just great before evil monsters began pouring out of the tunnels, and the chaos has claimed your mentor somewhere deep beneath the world. Being a fine, strapping hero you descend into the mines with your trusty (and capable) pet to fight, loot, explore, loot, fish, loot, and maybe get to the bottom of whatever’s going on. And collect some loot while you’re at it.

You’ll notice the connections to Diablo 1 the moment you load into town, and not just because the BGM there is a send-up of the Tristram theme. The structure of the game is identical, with you descending into a single, expansive, multi-level dungeon beneath the town to score loot and press on to the bosses in your way. Back in town you can sell your junk, buy new junk, mash your old junk into new junk, and give your junk new traits. It’s a familiar cycle, one that’s been expanded upon by virtually every ARPG that came after Diablo 1 (including its sequels), except for those that followed faithfully in its footsteps. I don’t consider this disqualifying, but taken alongside its other shortcomings it’s not a good look.

Combat is where you’ll spend the half of the game where you’re not futzing with loot, and it’s in a rough place between D1 and modern sensibilities. You’re certainly not snapped to a grid in these bright, colorful maps but your skills remain very stiff and not terribly exciting to use. I’ve gotten the farthest with the archer-style character who thankfully gets guns from the steampunk trappings of the setting, but ended up with no skills more interesting than exploding or ricocheting shots. The skill trees borrow from Diablo 2 in fact, expecting you to dump points into a main skill to spam all the time forever and ever. And keep in mind you’re going to be killing lots of very standard goblins and spiders with these skills, albeit very elaborately-designed ones.

What Torchlight has going for it, and what can save you from burning out on it after just a few hours, is a load of little side features that still support your ultimate goal of… well, finding loot, really. Your pet is a pretty big selling point on its own, starting you off with a doggie or kitty that you can eventually transmogrify into all kinds of adorable horrors. They can fight alongside you, get equipped with accessory items, hold extra items for you, and even cart junk back to town to sell while you forge ahead in the depths. There’s also fishing of all things that can turn up special items and buffs, and a portal to randomized challenge maps that can earn you important gear upgrades if you can make it to the end.

None of these elements are unique to Torchlight, of course, leaving the game feeling like a title cobbled together from the most visible bits of other games. Even the look is heavily cribbed from World of Warcraft, with great big technicolor shapes and over-designed armors and enemies. Time has only made these comparisons less favorable as the genre has moved forward with titles like Path of Exile and Grim Dawn, leaving Torchlight to stand as one of the better imitators of an outmoded game. That’s not the brightest crown to wear but it’s better than nothing, which is really the nicest thing I can say about this game in terms of a recommendation.

An interesting McGuffin, Ember is something that you can use to socket and enchant items, and it is what is being corrupted by something in the bottom of the mine. From the church, to catacombs, and then into hell; all blurred together. In this game you go from mines, to jungle ruins, to suddenly a library/necropolis, then to magma caves, then to dwarven ruins and finally some kind of weird demonic fortress? There really isn't any kind of cohesion to it or realistic progression.

The music for the town is lifted right from Diablo, and for the rest of the game it is passable. Honestly, the music and ambience isn't great, and I put my own music or podcasts over it. Torchlight, developed by Runic Games and released in 2009, is an action role-playing game that embraces the core tenets of the dungeon-crawling genre while infusing it with a distinctive charm, vibrant art style, and satisfying combat mechanics. While it doesn’t seek to radically reinvent the ARPG wheel, it excels at delivering a polished and accessible experience that captures the essence of loot-driven progression and hack-and-slash gameplay. In many ways, Torchlight feels like a spiritual successor to Diablo II, and that’s no accident—several of the game’s developers, including Travis Baldree and the Schaefer brothers, were key figures behind Blizzard’s genre-defining classic.

Set in the mining town of Torchlight, the game introduces players to a world where Ember, a powerful magical resource, is both a blessing and a curse. The narrative is relatively straightforward, functioning more as a backdrop than a focal point, but it does its job of motivating the player to descend into the depths below the town to uncover the source of growing corruption. While the story may lack the narrative complexity or emotional weight of modern RPGs, it leans into the genre's strengths by focusing on dungeon exploration, loot collection, and rapid-fire combat encounters.

Gameplay is where Torchlight shines most brightly. At the start, players choose from three character classes: the melee-focused Destroyer, the ranged and trap-savvy Vanquisher, and the spellcasting Alchemist. Each class has its own unique skill trees, allowing for diverse builds and playstyles. While the class selection is limited, the customization within each character’s development is robust, encouraging experimentation and replayability. The ability to specialize in different active and passive abilities offers meaningful decisions about combat strategy and character progression. Combat is fast, responsive, and satisfying—cleaving through hordes of monsters, watching colorful effects explode on screen, and collecting loot that showers out of defeated enemies gives every encounter a gratifying rhythm.

One of Torchlight’s most iconic features is its pet system. Players are accompanied by a faithful animal companion (a cat or a dog by default, though mods later expanded this selection) that can assist in combat, carry items, and even travel back to town to sell excess loot—eliminating the need for frequent breaks in dungeon diving. This mechanic is deceptively simple but greatly enhances the game’s pacing, allowing players to stay focused on exploration without excessive inventory micromanagement. It also adds a small but welcome layer of strategy, as pets can be equipped and even temporarily transformed using fish to gain special combat abilities.

Visually, Torchlight adopts a bold, stylized aesthetic that sets it apart from the grim and gritty tones of other ARPGs of its time. The bright, exaggerated art direction—reminiscent of a high-fantasy comic book—makes the world feel alive, even in the darkest depths of the mines. Monster designs are varied and imaginative, while spell effects and weapon animations maintain clarity and visual impact, even amid chaotic battles. Combined with a strong musical score by Matt Uelmen (another Diablo alum), which weaves together eerie ambient themes and epic battle music, the overall presentation is atmospheric and memorable.

Dungeon design in Torchlight is procedurally generated, ensuring that each playthrough offers a slightly different experience. The game’s central dungeon, which descends through a variety of distinct biome-like levels, grows more challenging and bizarre as players progress. From abandoned mines and ancient ruins to arcane laboratories and demonic lairs, each level introduces new enemies and hazards, keeping the experience from feeling repetitive. Optional side quests and randomly generated dungeons add extra layers of content and reward players who enjoy thorough exploration.

Loot, as expected in the genre, plays a central role, and Torchlight does not disappoint. Weapons, armor, rings, and other items come in a wide range of rarities and can include various magical properties. Players can also socket gear with Ember to enhance stats or grant new abilities, and the game features an enchanting system with a risk/reward component that allows for powerful gear upgrades at the cost of potential failure. The loot treadmill is tuned perfectly to keep players invested, as there’s always the possibility of a better item just around the corner.

Despite all its strengths, Torchlight isn’t without shortcomings. The lack of multiplayer was a notable omission at launch, especially given the genre’s strong tradition of cooperative play. Though the single-player experience is solid, some players might find it lacking in depth or longevity once they’ve exhausted the main dungeon. Additionally, enemy AI is fairly basic, and high-level combat can become repetitive without significantly new mechanics introduced later in the game. These limitations, however, are often outweighed by the game’s polish, accessibility, and charm.

In conclusion, Torchlight is a masterclass in streamlined action RPG design. It respects the legacy of its genre while making smart innovations that prioritize fun, pacing, and player engagement. Though it may not have the narrative ambition or sprawling multiplayer features of later entries, it delivers a focused and immensely satisfying dungeon-crawling experience that’s easy to pick up and difficult to put down. Whether you’re a veteran of the genre or a newcomer looking for a polished introduction to ARPGs, Torchlight remains a standout title well worth revisiting or discovering for the first time.

Torchlight, like its sequel, is a quite enjoyable ARPG dungeon-crawler with a lot of loot, fun, and exploration to be had! I've enjoyed this game since 2013, and although I haven't played it in a while, it, along with Torchlight II, are probably my favorite ARPG games!

The game is set in the small mining town of Torchlight, and the town needs help, as its mine is being attacked by monsters. As you continue further and further down the mine, you'll see a vast array of different enemies and environments, and quite a bit of loot to be had! 

There are three classes in Torchlight, and each one has different spells and weapon specializations. 

The Alchemist is a mage, specializing in staffs and wands, and has elemental spells and attacks. He has the highest MP of the classes.

The Destroyer is a melee-oriented class that is best at using swords, axes, maces, and polearms. He has the largest health pool of the classes.

The Vanquisher is a range-oriented class which has abilities that strengthen her ranged combat. She is best suited for long-range combat.

Torchlight is an enjoyable game to play, and and its visuals nice. Its soundtrack is excellent, as well, and compliments the game quite nicely, giving it its cool style, just like the sequel has a nice style. The environments in the game are pretty fascinating as well, and sometimes quite varied, and there's many places to explore, and some side quests to do too.

I also appreciate how lightweight it is, graphically. I think it still looks pretty good, while at the same time, being able to run even on old machines in my home, including old laptops!

Throughout the game, just like with its sequel, there is a huge variation of armor, weapons, and enchantments that you will find, and you can also transmute items and enchant things at an enchanter. You can also find "ember" to socket items, which gives you various bonuses.

Overall, I have no complaints about Torchlight. Its gameplay is very satisfying and quite fun, and I would certainly recommend this game, as well as its sequel, which introduces multiplayer co-op! Definitely pick both of them up, if you are someone who enjoys ARPGS, Co-op games, and loot games. ^.^

The lack of depth in skill progression makes the game feel like it’s missing one of the most essential parts of the genre.

Mobs
Monsters throughout the game only appear when you get close and vanish if you’re too far away.
Necromancers with 3-5 homing poison projectiles—Medea-like mobs that flood the path to Alric, spamming this skill with ridiculous damage scaling. Being able to tank the boss's damage but die to a normal mob is the peak of balance. 
Additionally, the game’s level design is filled with narrow corridors and stairs that obstruct your projectiles, making combat feel even more frustrating.
The levels feel extremely repetitive, with mobs using the same skills over and over.

Bosses
Most of the bosses up until the final one were relatively easy to defeat. However, the last boss takes a turn for the worse. Its sheer resilience and the constant spawning of minions make it unnecessarily difficult. 
What’s frustrating is the lack of clear mechanics or strategy to handle it; instead, you’re left grinding away, hoping the boss will eventually give in.

[h1] 𝕋𝕙𝕖 𝕞𝕠𝕣𝕖 "𝕦𝕟𝕤𝕖𝕣𝕚𝕠𝕦𝕤" 𝔻𝕚𝕒𝕓𝕝𝕠. [/h1]

Remember Diablo 1? A game where you're thrown into a barren village and you're given the vital task of descending a cathedral in search for the source of evil that's spawning creatures of all kinds from the demonic realm to torment the poor villagers? Welcome to Torchlight, a village that's quite similar in distress.

The villagers in Torchlight, however, do not even care about the evil that lurks in the bottom of the mines... They are more concerned with mundane activities, such as the alchemist who literally says "Nobody cares about whatever's in the mine, all I want is this gem, find it for me and I'll reward you". Between the funny villagers, the funny interactions with them and a plot that you won't care about, Torchlight offers little variety in questing.

To emphasize, remember how back in Diablo you've had, fetch quests alongside some creepy, scary "open this portal at your own risk" type of quests? Like how you'd read a curse on a book and then a huge scary demon with a horrifying voice spawns out of nowhere, calling you a "FRESH MEAT" before you're compelled to run away as fast as you can? Well... in Torchlight, the quests are... quests! Fetch this gem, go into this portal to fetch the flowers... Slay this guy, slay this one, slay that one... At some point, Torchlight will feel very fleshed out and boring. I know it is quintessential for any RPG to have those, but come on... descending four levels for a gem and a small portion of XP isn't even worth it. 

Anyways, the game's mechanics are nice; you could also dual-wield as a mage and die in two hits, the game doesn't really care as far as your character's customization goes. There are three classes, a fighter, an archer (of sorts) and a mage. The level design keeps changing the further you descend into the mines, the voice acting is not mediocre, but not good either... The soundtrack is great and then there's... the fishing! Apart from the endless optional dungeon you get after defeating the main game's final boss, the fishing in this game is the most-dragged out, the most-boring activity you could be doing while playing... You've got an average of thirty seconds to a whole minute waiting for a circle to align with the fish mark for you to click it and get the fish... It's just annoying as hell, and for an achievement you have to do it a thousand times! Nope... gotta draw the line somewhere boys...

Torchlight is a 7.2/10 Diablo-clone. It doesn't take its plot seriously (and that's, to me, a good thing) and has a ton of memorable characters as well as a horrid fishing mechanic that, in my opinion, should be deleted from the other entries.
The heavily stylized artstyle makes the game look nice even in 2025, despite the game being so old. The gameplay has also aged gracefully.

Both games go incredibly cheap on sales, a couple of euro/dollars if you want to wait. But I think both are worth it because they are both well made games from ex Diablo devs.

This is a neutral review. 

Torchlight is a classic of the Hack and Slash RPG genre. I didn't play it before, but I heard a lot about it. 
Well, it's a little dated, in terms of graphics and in terms of story paradigm (which is the basic - "the town is under threat by the dungeons full of monsters below it!"). 

It's very entertaining and addictive. But only to people like me who are fans of this type of games. Gamers who are not into hack and slash RPGs will definetely find Torchlight very repetitive. It's basically one dungeon after the other, until the 35th floor where the final boss awaits you. You can even play after the final boss for an infinite amount of subsequent floors. The dungeons are always randomly created, every subsequent floor is larger then the previous one. 
There are only 3 classes - fighter, rogue and wizard. The variety of weapons and skills is ok, but I have seen better skill trees. It's better to max level just a few skill instead of wasting the skill points on too many skills. The thing I didn't like is that you really have to know which skills are best if you want to have an easier time in this game. So you need to research your class before starting to play. 
I found the game too easy on Normal, and on Hard it's challenging only in the last levels and final boss. But maybe I had luck with the random loot drops. 

The enemy variety is also just ok (not great), and the poor graphics doesn't let you distinguish them enough. 
Make no mistake, this was a very good game at the time of production, even in 2024 I had fun with it, but it clearly didn't age very well. 
A good example why it didn't age well is the quest paradigm that consist of the same 3 type of quests that recycle all the time. Also there are no extra events or locations that would break the dungeon/leveling up monotony.

The single player predecessor of Torchlight II, offers solid dungeon crawling gameplay reminiscent of the good old Diablo II days. With 3 main classes to select with a range a different skills and abilities, the game offers a multitude of gameplay experiences, with a permenant-death hardcore mode for the dedicated gamers. Fan created Mods offer various new styles of gameplay with additional pets, classes, skills, NPCs and more. Torchlight created a great fan base for its popular bigger brother, which I no doubt look forward to playing. 

Pros:
+ Nice variety of player skills
+ Fan created mods add plenty of replayability
+ Added difficulty settings and a Hardcore mode for an extra challenge
+ A wide variety of achievments to complete
+ Good to zone out for mindless monster killing after a tiring day at the office

Cons:
- Many achievements are very tedious and grindy
- Fishing is awful
- The dungeons and enemies themselves can get repetitive after a while

Furthermore, you aren't really forced to evolve your character further and further. You can keep the same skills and just invest more points into them.
